title: How Long Should Each Slide Stay on Screen in a Video? (blog explainer)

brief.story: A clear explainer of the post.

slides.title: How long should each slide stay on screen?
slides.notes: In a video, viewers can't ask you to slow down. Get slide timing right and it feels calm and clear. Get it wrong, and it drags or rushes.

slides.title: Let the narration decide
bullets: As long as it takes to say, plus a beat
slides.notes: There's no single correct number. Keep each slide up as long as it takes to say what it's about, plus a short pause. The words set the rhythm.

slides.title: Practical ranges by slide type
slides.notes: Use these as starting points, then adjust after the preview. If a slide needs more than about forty-five seconds, it's probably carrying two ideas. Split it.

slides.title: Split one long slide into three
bullets: After: three slides, 15 to 20 seconds each
Report to the privacy team within one hour
Use the breach form, not email
slides.notes: A breach reporting slide sat still for over a minute while viewers drifted. As three slides, the total length stayed similar, but every topic change brought a new visual.

slides.title: Fix slides that feel rushed or stale
bullets: Too long: split it or reveal parts as you go
Too short: add a sentence of narration
One to three sentences per simple slide
slides.notes: If a slide drags, split it or reveal each part as the narration reaches it. If it flashes past, add a sentence so viewers get a fair look.

slides.title: Watch it, then tune the timing
bullets: Speaker notes set each slide's time
slides.notes: Speaker notes set the timing. On Pro, a.i. directs the video, pacing each scene to your narration. Try Basic first at powerpoint2vid.com.
